Marisol Vega

gap-017 · supplement · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I like when everybody knows what they're doing and you can tell if the team got it done. I'm not the person who remembers every big word first. I can practice something a lot without getting tired of it, though. People say I'm confident because I'm loud. Sometimes I'm loud because I don't know what else to do. I still want my friends to think I'm fun.

  • family: Lives with her mother, grandmother, and younger brother; parents separated amicably and father lives nearby.
  • finances: Modest but stable income; several relatives coordinate transport and occasional costs.
  • geography: San Antonio, Texas; extended family concentrated in nearby neighborhoods.
  • cultureLanguages: Mexican American; English at school, mixed English and Spanish with family; regular large family celebrations.
  • school: Large public high school; average grades and strong attendance; participates in an emergency-response youth program.
  • accessOpportunities: School athletics and a city-supported youth response program; access depends on shared rides and borrowed equipment.
  • Age 4–5

    Marisol liked being assigned a job during family gatherings, especially carrying napkins where everyone could see her helping. She also interrupted cousins' games when she thought they were excluding her. Her grandmother kept a predictable afternoon routine of snacks, television, and a walk. Marisol learned the neighbors' names because she liked stopping to talk along the route.

  • Age 6–7

    At elementary school she was eager to be line leader and disappointed when she had to wait her turn. Reading came easily enough, while handwriting annoyed her. Her mother enrolled her in a low-cost soccer program. Marisol liked the noisy sideline encouragement and the feeling of belonging to a named team more than practicing alone in the yard.

  • Age 8–9

    A firefighter visited her classroom and demonstrated protective equipment. Marisol remembered the radio chatter and the way people checked each other's gear. She did not immediately announce a future occupation. That year she mainly wanted a glittery phone case and permission to stay up for a television finale. Her friendships involved frequent arguments that were forgotten by recess.

  • Age 10–11

    During a neighborhood power outage she accompanied her grandmother to check on an older neighbor. She liked having a clear, finite task: carry a charged lantern and bring back the empty one. Later she repeated the story enough that her brother rolled his eyes. At school she struggled with fractions and needed repeated examples before a procedure stuck.

  • Age 12–13

    Marisol moved into a larger middle school and became self-conscious about being taller than most friends. Soccer gave her a place where her body felt useful, although she disliked photographs posted after games. She sometimes joined classmates in mocking a girl's awkward messages and felt uncomfortable when adults discussed online kindness. She has never directly repaired that relationship.

  • Age 14–15

    A cousin invited her to a youth emergency-response demonstration. Marisol joined the following term, enjoying equipment checks, radio practice, and timed group exercises. She was slower at recalling unfamiliar terminology than some teammates. When nervous, she spoke too quickly over the radio. A patient leader rehearsed with her until she could deliver short messages at a usable pace.

  • Age 16

    At sixteen she helps prepare practice stations and reliably brings the attendance list. She likes exercises with coordinated roles and an obvious finish. She is less interested in reading lengthy manuals at home. Her mother worries about dangerous work and promotes college programs with predictable hours. Marisol has not decided whether her response interest belongs in her future or just her present weekends.

Life now

  • enjoys: Coordinated practical drills · Team banter · Family parties · Soccer games
  • avoids: Long technical manuals · Being photographed after sports · Working alone on open-ended projects
  • activities: Youth emergency-response practice · Recreational soccer · Helping grandmother with errands
  • demonstratedSkills: Checks equipment against a list · Passes brief practiced radio messages · Keeps track of group attendance · Maintains effort during physical drills
  • unfamiliarActivities: Actual emergency response · Advanced first-aid decisions · Independent laboratory work · Office systems beyond school software
  • motivations: Being trusted with a role · Team belonging · Visible progress
  • ambitions: Interested in doing something active with a dependable team · Also wants college because her mother considers it essential
  • struggles: Technical vocabulary retention · Body-image discomfort in photographs · Uneasy unresolved peer behavior
  • supports: Grandmother and both parents · Patient youth-program leader · Cousin who introduced the program
  • practicalConstraints: Shared rides · Some program fees require planning · Time split with soccer and family

Still uncertain: Will she sustain interest when activities involve more study and less group excitement? · How does she respond to a role without visible recognition? · Can she address the unresolved harm in her former peer group?
